transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-03-26 11:00 PT / 14:00 ET
- Duration: ~45 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (CTO, NovaRetail), Ethan Park (ML Eng), Ravi Singh (Infra), Leah Gomez (Product)

Summary:
Weekly POC sync to review latest latency/throughput benchmarks comparing Redwood Dedicated profile with NovaRetail's baseline provider. Discussed tuning (KV cache, batching, quantization), networking variance, and next steps for an RPS stress run. Agreed on spreadsheet updates and action owners.

Topics:
- 99th percentile latency gaps across models and sequence lengths
- Throughput delta under sustained high RPS and burst conditions
- Config knobs: KV cache, continuous batching windows, quantization profile (int8 vs q4f16-ish), autoscale behavior
- Networking variance and VPC peering impact on p95/p99
- Cost comparison methodology vs baseline provider

Action items (recorded in doc and as verbal): see metadata above

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, uh welcome back to the weekly POC sync, thanks for making time. Quick roll call, we got NovaRetail, correct?
[00:08] Sofia Martinez: Yep, hi Alex, thanks, Sofia here. We got Ethan, Ravi and Leah on from my side.
[00:13] Alex: Great. I'll hand it to Priya for the benchmark walkthrough.
[00:18] Priya Patel: Cool, thanks. So we ran the updated bench across the three models you asked for, small-medium-large, and compared Redwood Dedicated with your baseline provider. High level: median latency is basically comparable on short seqs, but we're seeing a consistent 15-25% improvement on throughput at sustained RPS on the Dedicated pool. The p99 though—so 99th percentile—is mixed, there's a tail in a few runs that lines up with network hiccups.
[00:45] Ethan Park: Can you unpack the p99 delta a bit? Like is that GPU scheduling, batching, or network?
[00:51] Priya: Yeah, good question. We instrumented the runtime. Roughly breakdown: about 40% of the p99 excess on one of the medium model runs was wait on KV cache miss cascades, 30% looks like transient GC/host memory pressure on the baseline provider side, and 30% is network latency variance—VPC peering jitter—so it's kinda split. When we enabled persistent KV caching and bumped batching windows slightly, the p99 improved by ~120-160 ms on the test runs.
[01:25] Ravi Singh: Those KV cache misses—are they because of the request distribution? Our traffic has a long tail of sessions.
[01:30] Priya: Exactly, we saw a cold prefix fraction—about 18%—where the KV didn't hit. For your cart/session flows if you can give the exact seq length histogram we'll tune eviction and prefetch strategies.
[01:40] Ethan: I'll send anonymized seq histogram, should have it by Monday.
[01:43] Leah Gomez: Are the throughput numbers with quantization enabled? We saw model quality drift earlier when you suggested q4 variants.
[01:49] Marcus Lee: Good catch. For this run we had two configurations: baseline quant (fp16) and a q4f16-like profile for the medium model. Quality was checked on the 200-sample eval set you provided; we didn't see statistically significant regression for the medium model on the q4 profile, but for large model there was a slight drop in relevancy scores, so we left large on fp16 for now.
[02:17] Sofia: Ok so for large we keep fp16; for medium we can try q4 if it keeps the latency down but we need to watch relevancy. Can you add a small eval on cart-edge cases?
[02:26] Marcus: Yep we'll add the cart-edge set, please send the additional queries you mentioned, Leah.
[02:31] Leah: Will do.
[02:33] Alex: On networking, Ravi, you mentioned earlier you were testing the VPC peering setup—any notes?
[02:38] Ravi: Yeah, thanks. We saw about 20–40 ms variance when traffic went across peering during our internal tests. On Redwood's Dedicated we still see a net lower tail in most runs but that peering jitter explains the occasional spikes. If we move the test nodes into the same AZ for the RPS run we should reduce that.
[02:56] Priya: Agreed. Also worth noting that Redwood's smart routing will keep requests local to the Dedicated pool where possible; the spikes are only when the test harness crosses boundaries.
[03:05] Ethan: One thing—your throughput numbers looked better, but cost per token looked higher in one sensitivity slice. How are you calculating cost vs baseline?
[03:12] Alex: Good question. We're including GPU time plus amortized infra and license for Dedicated. For the hosted per-token numbers we did token * rate math; for Dedicated we estimated monthly commit amortized across provisioned throughput. We'll push a breakdown spreadsheet with assumptions.
[03:25] Sofia: We'll need the per-route breakdown, e.g., short chat vs long generation. That's how procurement will parse it.
[03:31] Alex: Yep we'll include per-route.
[03:33] Priya: Back to tuning—two quick experiments we recommend: enable persistent KV cache for the warm subset and test with continuous batching window of 25ms vs 50ms. For your traffic shape the 25ms window reduced mean latency by 40ms and slightly increased throughput. But if you favor p99 we saw 50ms sometimes helps because it batches more. So it's tradeoff.
[03:55] Ethan: So 25ms for latency-sensitive, 50ms for throughput-sensitive. Any automatic adaptive option?
[04:00] Priya: We're working on a dynamic window feature but not in this POC. For now we can script autoscale policies to switch profiles during peak windows.
[04:08] Leah: About logs and auditing—we need audit logs and token-level tracing for cost allocation. Is that already in the Dedicated trial?
[04:15] Alex: Yes, the Dedicated trial includes token-level cost breakdowns and trace ids; we'll give you access to the console and show how to map traces to routes.
[04:23] Ravi: Great. Also for the upcoming RPS run, should we expect warm caches? I want repeatable conditions.
[04:29] Priya: We'll do warm-up rounds to reach steady-state. We'll run 3 warm-up passes and then the measurement window. We'll also capture kernel-level timing and the KV hit/miss logs.
[04:38] Sofia: Timeline check—can we do the RPS run early April?
[04:41] Alex: Yes, aiming week of April 6th. We'll coordinate with Ethan and Ravi for AZ placement.
[04:46] Ethan: I'll update the test harness and share the endpoint config by Monday.
[04:49] Priya: Quick note on edge cases—during one of the medium model runs we saw a scheduling preemption when an ephemeral maintenance job kicked in on the node. We pushed a change to avoid background jobs during bench windows and re-ran; that removed the outlier. We'll keep bench nodes isolated.
[05:08] Marcus: Also, for transparency, we compared p50/p95/p99 across different seq lengths: short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-256), long (256-1024). Redwood had about 10–18% throughput advantage on medium and long under sustained load. Short seqs were pretty even.
[05:28] Leah: From product perspective, the key success criteria for us: p99 under 500ms for medium flows at 200 RPS, and cost per 1M tokens under $X (TBD). We're close on latency but need the RPS run to validate.
[05:40] Alex: We'll aim to demonstrate that SLA in the run.
[05:43] Sofia: Any blockers for procurement/legal? We will need SOC2 docs.
[05:47] Alex: We already shared the SOC2 and security pack last week; I'll re-send with the bench artifacts.
[05:53] Sofia: Awesome.
[05:55] Alex: Alright, quick recap of next steps: Priya runs and shares the KV cache p99 stress logs (due Mon 3/29), Ethan provides seq histogram (due 3/30), Alex shares pricing and cost spreadsheet (due 4/02), schedule live RPS run week of 4/6. Anything else?
[06:12] Ethan: I'll add the cart-edge queries and send them by Monday.
[06:15] Leah: I'll coordinate product acceptance criteria and share them in the doc.
[06:18] Alex: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the thread with the updated bench sheet and calendar invite for the RPS run.
[06:24] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hears around internal kernel names and q4 variants; speaker turns sometimes overlap in the recording so a couple of lines attributed to general speaker were normalized to names.
